q: Every reaction has a rate, or speed, at which it proceeds.
e: True. Every reaction has a rate, or speed, at which it proceeds. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Different chemical reactions occur at the same rate.
e: False. Different reactions run at very different rates. Rusting is slow; explosions are fast.

q: Weathering of rocks happens within a second.
e: False. Weathering of rocks is a very slow reaction. It takes years, not a second.

q: The study of reaction rate is known as chemical thermodynamics.
e: False. The study of reaction rates is chemical kinetics. Thermodynamics is about energy and equilibrium, not how fast.

q: An iron nail reacts rapidly in the air as it rusts.
e: False. An iron nail rusts slowly in air. Rapid would not be the word for ordinary rusting.

q: The reaction rate is usually expressed as the change in the amount of a reactant used up or the product formed in a unit of volume.
e: False. Rate is change in concentration, or amount per unit volume, per unit time. Leaving time out of the definition is the mistake.

q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid giving off oxygen gas.
e: False. Magnesium and hydrochloric acid give hydrogen gas. Oxygen is not the gas from that metal-acid reaction.

q: The rate of disappearance of $Mg$ is expressed as mass of $Mg$ reacted divided by time.
e: True. The rate of disappearance of Mg is expressed as mass of Mg reacted divided by time. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The rate of formation of $H_2$ is expressed as volume of $H_2$ collected divided by time.
e: True. The rate of formation of H2 is expressed as volume of H2 collected divided by time. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: If the substance is a gas, the amount consumed or formed is expressed in pressure units or as measured in volume.
e: True. If the substance is a gas, the amount consumed or formed is expressed in pressure units or as measured in volume. Raising the pressure of a gas crushes more particles into the same volume and can speed collisions.

q: Concentration units are used if the reactant or product is in the gaseous state.
e: False. Gases are often followed in partial pressure. Concentration units are the usual choice for solutions.

q: The time measurement is expressed in whatever units fit the reaction.
e: True. The time measurement is expressed in whatever units fit the reaction. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: Generally, the rate of a reaction in solution is measured in terms of a decrease in the concentration of the reactant per unit time at a constant temperature.
e: True. Generally, the rate of a reaction in solution is measured in terms of a decrease in the concentration of the reactant per unit time at a constant temperature. Higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions.

q: The rate of reactant used up is expressed as $+\frac{\Delta[\text{reactant}]}{\Delta t}$.
e: False. Reactant concentration falls, so the rate of use is written with a minus sign. The plus sign would describe product appearing.

q: The rate of product formed is expressed as $+\frac{\Delta[\text{product}]}{\Delta t}$.
e: True. The rate of product formed is expressed as +delta [product]delta t. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The delta ($\Delta$) means change and the square bracket $[]$ represents molar concentration.
e: True. The delta (delta) means change and the square bracket [] represents molar concentration. Higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions.

q: The minus sign in the rate expression means an increase in the concentration of the reactant.
e: False. The minus sign is there because reactant concentration is decreasing. An increase would not need that minus.

q: Rate is expressed as a positive quantity.
e: True. Rate is expressed as a positive quantity. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The rate constant $k$ explains the relationship between the molar concentration of the reactants and the rate of a chemical reaction.

q: The mole ratios from the balanced chemical equation cannot be used to determine the rates of change in concentrations of products and reactants.
e: False. Stoichiometric mole ratios are exactly how you convert one species' rate into another's. The balanced equation is required for that.

q: In the reaction $Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow ZnCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)$, the rate of disappearance of $HCl$ is half the rate of disappearance of $Zn$.
e: False. Two HCl are used for each Zn, so HCl disappears twice as fast as Zn, not half as fast.
